This document explains the checks of our final ordered logit model and what
we conclude from each of them. The checks are run by
`scripts/06c_ordered_logit_checks.R`, and this document only reads the tables
that script saves in `outputs/tables/ologit_check_*.csv`. How the model is
built and fitted is explained in `06_ordered_logit_documentation.qmd`.

To render it, run `01_clean.R`, `03_train_test_split.R`,
`06a_ordered_logit_full_model.R` and `06c_ordered_logit_checks.R` first, then:

```bash
quarto render scripts/06c_ordered_logit_checks_documentation.qmd
```

```{r setup}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
```

```{r data}
library(dplyr)
rd  <- function(f) read.csv(file.path("outputs/tables", f))
po    <- rd("ologit_check_po.csv")
ppo   <- rd("ologit_check_ppo.csv")
lin   <- rd("ologit_check_linearity.csv")
lin_o <- rd("ologit_check_linearity_other.csv")
gvif  <- rd("ologit_check_gvif.csv")
rob   <- rd("ologit_check_robustness.csv")

# the main determinants, used to summarise how much they change
key_terms <- c("hincfel", "health", "stfeco", "partner", "female",
               "activity_grpUnemployed", "cntryLV")
r1 <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
```

# What is checked

The model is M3: an ordered logit for `stflife` (0--10) with all 22 group
predictors plus the Latvia round 10 indicator `lv_r10`, weighted with
`anweight`, with design-based standard errors. It is fitted on **all data**
(train + test, 12,688 respondents), the fit whose odds ratios go into the
report. Every check below is run on this fit.

There are two kinds of checks.

* **Assumption checks** ask whether an ordered logit fits these data: does
  each predictor have the same effect at every point of the scale
  (proportional odds), do numeric predictors have equal steps (linearity), and
  are the predictors too strongly related to each other (multicollinearity)?
  The fourth usual assumption, independent observations, does not hold in a
  clustered survey, which is why all standard errors are design-based.
* **Robustness checks** ask whether the results depend on choices we made:
  the 80/20 split, filling in missing values, and the Latvia round 10 survey.

The checks cannot prove that the model is right. They show whether its
assumptions hold well enough and whether the conclusions change.

## Summary

```{r summary}
po_var <- po %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(spread = max(spread)) %>%
  arrange(desc(spread))
ppo_vars <- po_var$variable[po_var$spread > 0.5]
lin_t <- lin %>% group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(dAIC = first(dAIC), p = first(p), max_gap = max(abs(gap)),
            slope_total = abs(last(linear_effect))) %>% arrange(desc(dAIC))
nonlin <- lin_t$variable[lin_t$dAIC > 10]
rob_c <- filter(rob, type == "coefficient")
rob_k <- filter(rob_c, term %in% key_terms)

summ <- data.frame(
  Check = c("Proportional odds", "Linearity", "Multicollinearity",
            "Robustness (3 refits)"),
  Result = c(
    paste0("Violated for ", length(ppo_vars), " variables. Freeing them changes the other odds ratios by at most ",
           r1(max(abs(ppo$OR_change_pct))), "%."),
    paste0("Not linear for ", length(nonlin), " attitude scales. Coding them as categories changes the main determinants by at most ",
           r1(max(abs(lin_o$OR_change_pct[lin_o$term %in% key_terms]))), "%."),
    paste0("Highest GVIF^(1/(2 df)) ", round(max(gvif$GVIF_adj), 2), ", well below 2.2."),
    paste0(sum(rob_c$alt_in_ref_ci), " of ", nrow(rob_c),
           " refitted estimates lie inside the 95% CI of the final model. Main determinants change by at most ",
           r1(max(abs(rob_k$OR_change_pct))), "%.")),
  Conclusion = c("Report average effects", "Limitation, keep numeric",
                 "No problem", "Results are robust"))
knitr::kable(summ)
```

**Overall conclusion.** The model's assumptions hold well enough for its main
conclusions. Two assumptions are broken (proportional odds for some variables
and linearity for the attitude scales), but neither changes the effects of
income, health and the other main determinants. The results also do not
depend on the train/test split, on filling in missing values or on the
Latvia round 10 survey.

# Assumption checks

## Proportional odds

**What it is.** The ordered logit gives each predictor one odds ratio for the
whole 0--10 scale. It assumes, for example, that income raises the odds of
scoring above 4 by the same factor as the odds of scoring above 8.

**How we checked it.** We fitted separate yes/no (binary) logits for
"score of at least $k$" at $k$ = 5, 7, 8 and 9, with the same predictors. If
the assumption holds, the coefficients are similar across the four cut-offs.
The spread is the largest minus the smallest of them, on the log-odds scale.
With 12,688 respondents a formal test rejects the assumption for almost any
variable, so we look at the size of the spread and, more importantly, at
whether the violation changes the other results.

```{r po}
knitr::kable(po_var %>% mutate(spread = round(spread, 2)),
             col.names = c("Variable", "Largest spread (log-odds)"))
```

**Result.** The assumption holds well for the main determinants (income,
health, trust, the satisfaction ratings, partner and gender, spreads of
`r round(max(po_var$spread[po_var$variable %in% c("hincfel", "health", "trstprl", "ppltrst", "stfeco", "stfhlth", "partner", "female")]), 2)`
or less). It is violated (spread above 0.5) for
`r paste(ppo_vars, collapse = ", ")`. For example, meeting people
(`sclmeet`) matters more for moving out of the lowest scores than for reaching
the highest ones.

**Does it matter?** We refitted the model once for each of these variables,
giving that variable a separate effect at every cut-off (a partial
proportional odds model, `ordinal::clm`), and compared the odds ratios of all
other variables with the final model. One variable at a time, because freeing
several at once gives an invalid fit.

```{r ppo}
ppo %>% group_by(nominal) %>%
  summarise(median = median(abs(OR_change_pct)), largest = max(abs(OR_change_pct)),
            key = max(abs(OR_change_pct[term %in% key_terms]))) %>%
  mutate(across(-nominal, ~ round(.x, 1))) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Variable freed", "Median change (%)",
                             "Largest change (%)", "Main determinants, largest (%)"))
```

**Conclusion.** The other odds ratios change by a median of
`r r1(median(abs(ppo$OR_change_pct)))`% and at most
`r r1(max(abs(ppo$OR_change_pct)))`%. The violations do not bias the other
effects, so the model keeps one effect per variable. For the variables that
break the assumption, the odds ratio is an average effect over the scale.

## Linearity of the numeric predictors

**What it is.** A numeric predictor gets one odds ratio per unit, which
assumes every step has the same effect (for example, from 2 to 3 the same as
from 8 to 9 on trust in parliament).

**How we checked it.** Each numeric predictor was entered as a category
variable (one effect per value) instead of a number, one at a time. If the
category version fits much better (AIC lower by more than 10), the steps are
not equal. The largest gap compares the two versions at any value, against the
whole linear effect from the lowest to the highest value.

```{r lin}
lin_t %>% mutate(dAIC = round(dAIC, 1), p = format(signif(p, 2), scientific = TRUE),
                 max_gap = round(max_gap, 2), slope_total = round(slope_total, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Variable", "AIC gain as categories", "p (LR test)",
                             "Largest gap (log-odds)", "Whole linear effect (log-odds)"))
```

**Result.** Income (`hincfel`) and health are close to linear. The factor
version fits clearly better for `r paste(nonlin, collapse = ", ")`. The
0--10 attitude scales all have the same shape: nearly flat over most of the
scale and a jump at 8--10, largest at 10.

```{r shape, fig.height = 3.2, fig.width = 7}
sh <- filter(lin, variable %in% c("stfeco", "stfhlth", "trstprl"))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (v in c("stfeco", "stfhlth", "trstprl")) {
  x <- filter(sh, variable == v)
  plot(x$level, x$factor_effect, type = "b", pch = 16, main = v,
       xlab = "Value", ylab = "Effect vs 0 (log-odds)",
       ylim = range(c(x$factor_effect, x$linear_effect)))
  lines(x$level, x$linear_effect, lty = 2)
}
par(op)
```

*Solid: effect of each value as a category. Dashed: the linear effect in the
model.*

This pattern probably reflects a response style: people who answer 10 on
other questions also tend to give high life satisfaction scores. It also
explains why trust in parliament has almost no average effect in M3 (OR close
to 1), while people with complete trust (10) are clearly more satisfied.

**Does it matter?** We refitted the model with all of these scales as
categories at once and compared the other odds ratios.

```{r lin-other}
lin_o %>% filter(term %in% key_terms) %>%
  mutate(across(c(OR_M3, OR_factors), ~ round(.x, 3)),
         OR_change_pct = round(OR_change_pct, 1)) %>%
  select(term, OR_M3, OR_factors, OR_change_pct) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Term", "OR, final model", "OR, scales as categories", "Change (%)"))
```

**Conclusion.** The main determinants change by at most
`r r1(max(abs(lin_o$OR_change_pct[lin_o$term %in% key_terms])))`% (all other
terms: median `r r1(median(abs(lin_o$OR_change_pct)))`%). We keep the scales
numeric, read their odds ratios as average trends and report the non-linearity
as a limitation.

## Multicollinearity

**What it is.** If predictors are strongly related to each other, their
separate effects are hard to estimate and their standard errors grow.

**How we checked it.** Generalised variance inflation factors from a weighted
linear model with the same predictors. $\text{GVIF}^{1/(2\,df)}$ makes
category variables comparable with single terms. Values above about 2.2 (the
square root of the usual cut-off 5) would be a concern.

```{r gvif}
knitr::kable(head(gvif, 6) %>% mutate(across(c(GVIF, GVIF_adj), ~ round(.x, 2))),
             col.names = c("Variable", "GVIF", "df", "GVIF^(1/(2 df))"))
```

**Conclusion.** The highest value is `r round(max(gvif$GVIF_adj), 2)`
(`r gvif$variable[1]`), well below 2.2. Multicollinearity is not a problem.
Satisfaction with the economy is related to trust in parliament, but not
strongly enough to make the estimates unstable.

# Robustness checks

Each check refits the final model on different rows and compares every odds
ratio with the final model. The refits share most of their rows with the
final model, so the differences are described, not tested.

1. **Train set only:** the model fitted on the 80% train set (`06a`) instead
   of all data. Shows whether the estimates depend on the 80/20 split.
2. **Complete cases only:** without the 1,348 respondents for whom a missing
   predictor was filled in (median or mode) in `03_train_test_split.R`. Shows
   whether filling in missing values changes the estimates.
3. **Without Latvia round 10:** that survey was self-completed rather than
   face-to-face. The model handles it with the `lv_r10` indicator, which only
   shifts the level of life satisfaction in that group. Dropping the group
   shows whether the survey mode also distorts the effects.

```{r rob}
labels <- c(train_only = "1. Train set only", complete_cases = "2. Complete cases",
            without_lv_r10 = "3. Without Latvia R10")
rob_c %>% group_by(check) %>%
  summarise(inside = paste(sum(alt_in_ref_ci), "of", n()),
            median = median(abs(OR_change_pct)),
            key = max(abs(OR_change_pct[term %in% key_terms])),
            se = median(se_ratio),
            sig = sum(sig_change)) %>%
  arrange(match(check, names(labels))) %>%
  mutate(check = labels[check], across(c(median, key), ~ round(.x, 1)),
         se = round(se, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Check", "Inside final 95% CI", "Median OR change (%)",
                             "Main determinants, largest (%)", "Median SE ratio",
                             "Significance changes"))
```

The main determinants in each version:

```{r rob-key}
wide <- rob_k %>% select(check, term, OR_ref, OR_alt) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = check, values_from = OR_alt)
knitr::kable(wide, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Term", "Final model", labels[names(wide)[-(1:2)]]))
```

**Result.** Every refitted estimate lies inside the 95% confidence interval of
the final model. The SE ratio is close to what the change in sample size alone
would give (for example, about 1.12 for the train set). The only changes in
significance are for effects with p-values near 0.05 in the final model.

**Conclusion.** The results do not depend on the split, on filling in missing
values or on the Latvia round 10 survey. Effects with p-values near 0.05
(Estonia compared with Lithuania, the oldest age group, speaking Russian at
home, single levels of education, area and social activity) are not stable
across the checks and should not be presented as findings.

# Limitations for the report

* The 0--10 attitude scales are not linear. Their odds ratios are average
  trends.
* For country, age, activity and meeting people the effect differs along the
  scale. Their odds ratios are average effects.
* `stfeco` and `stfhlth` are satisfaction ratings close to the outcome. They
  absorb part of the effects of trust, income and health, and the country
  effects are those among people who rate the economy equally.
* Some choices were made after seeing the data (`lv_r10`, the household size
  cap), and missing predictors were filled in with the median or mode. The
  robustness checks show that the conclusions do not depend on them.
* All results are associations, not causal effects.
